choices.text: They weigh the same, because both are one mole
Hydrogen weighs 1 g and oxygen weighs 16 g
Hydrogen weighs 16 g and oxygen weighs 1 g

questions.feedback: If you picked they weigh the same, that is the trap: One mole of anything weighs the same. Reteach point: Mass = moles x molar mass: one mole of hydrogen is 1 g but one mole of oxygen is 16 g. A mole fixes the number of particles, not the mass.
questions.misconception: One mole of anything weighs the same.
questions.prompt: One mole of hydrogen atoms and one mole of oxygen atoms are compared. What is true about their masses?

questions.answer: A mole is a counting word for 6.02 × 10²³ particles, just as a dozen is a counting word for 12 items.
questions.feedback: A strong answer calls the mole a counting word and gives the number 6.02 × 10²³ particles. An answer that gives a mass in grams is mixing up the count with the molar mass.
questions.prompt: In one sentence, explain what a mole is.

questions.feedback: Use n = m / M: 24 g / 12 g/mol = 2 mol. If you answered 24 mol, you used the mass alone without dividing by the molar mass.
questions.prompt: How many moles are there in 24 g of carbon-12? (Molar mass = 12 g/mol)

questions.answer: 1 mol of oxygen, because the mole ratio in 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O is 2 : 1 : 2, so 2 mol of hydrogen reacts with half as many moles of oxygen.
questions.feedback: The equation counts moles in the ratio 2 : 1 : 2: the oxygen moles are always half the hydrogen moles in this reaction. Do not use grams in the ratio - convert to moles first.
questions.prompt: In the reaction 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, how many moles of oxygen react with 2 mol of hydrogen? Explain your answer.
